BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

In the Matter of the Application of:              )
                                                  )
DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC                 )               Docket No. P-15424-000


                    CONSERVATION LAW FOUNDATION
           COMMENTS OPPOSING PRELIMINARY PERMIT APPLICATION

       On February 11, 2026, DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC (DeepGreen) filed an

application for a preliminary permit under Section 4(f) of the Federal Power Act; DeepGreen

modified and supplemented its application on June 8, 2026 and July 30, 2026. 1 In its application,

DeepGreen proposed to study the feasibility of the DeepGreen Western Passage Subsea-Compute

& Infrastructure Hub Project No. 15424-000 (Underwater Data Center). 2 The proposed

Underwater Data Center would be located in the Bay of Fundy, near the City of Eastport,

Maine. 3 On August 19, 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) accepted the

application for filing and requested public comment. 4

       Conservation Law Foundation submits these comments in opposition to DeepGreen’s

preliminary permit application. The comments raise two main arguments. First, given the

likelihood of a statewide ban or other limitations on data center construction in Maine as well as

the City of Eastport’s disapproval of the Underwater Data Center specifically, it would be

unreasonable and inefficient to grant DeepGreen’s application. Second, the proposed project




1
  Fed. Energy Regul. Comm’n Docket P-15424-000, Notice of Preliminary Permit Application Accepted
for Filing and Soliciting Comments, Motions to Intervene, and Competing Applications 1 (Aug. 19,
2026).
2
  Id.
3
  Id.
4
  Id.

 should not proceed due to the negative impacts on the marine ecosystem, including on critically

endangered North Atlantic right whales and several commercially important fish species.

    I.      Given the Likelihood of Statewide Restrictions on Data Center Construction and
            Local Opposition to the Underwater Data Center, Granting DeepGreen’s
            Preliminary Permit Application Would Be Unreasonable and Inefficient.

         Water power developers regulated by the Federal Power Act sometimes lack the Section 9

information needed to apply for a project license. To address this problem, Section 4(f)

authorizes FERC to issue a preliminary permit to a project developer. 5 The preliminary permit

“secure[s] priority of application for a license for a water power project . . . while the permittee

obtains the data and performs the acts required to determine the feasibility of the project and to

support an application for a license.” 6 If a project developer is unlikely to meet Section 9’s

requirements for a license, however, granting a preliminary permit under Section 4(f) is illogical

and specious.

         Such is the case here. DeepGreen seeks a preliminary permit under Section 4(f) to study

the proposed Underwater Data Center’s feasibility. 7 But under Section 9, to receive a license

from FERC to actually build the Underwater Data Center, DeepGreen would also need to submit

“[s]atisfactory evidence” that it has complied with Maine law “with respect to bed and banks and

to the appropriation, diversion, and use of water for power purposes and with respect to the right

to engage in the business of developing, transmitting, and distributing power, and in any other




5
  16 U.S.C. § 797(f).
6
  18 CFR § 4.80; see also 16 U.S.C. § 798(a) (“Each preliminary permit issued under this subchapter shall
be for the sole purpose of maintaining priority of application for a license under the terms of this chapter
for such period or periods, not exceeding a total of 4 years, as in the discretion of the Commission may be
necessary for making examinations and surveys, for preparing maps, plans, specifications, and estimates,
and for making financial arrangements.”).
7
  Fed. Energy Regul. Comm’n Docket P-15424-000, Notice of Preliminary Permit Application Accepted
for Filing and Soliciting Comments, Motions to Intervene, and Competing Applications 1 (Aug. 19,
2026).
                                                     2
 business necessary to effect the purposes of a license under this Act.” 8 As explained below,

DeepGreen cannot reasonably provide such evidence given the probability of a statewide ban or

other significant limitation on data center construction as well as the City of Eastport’s existing

moratorium. It would therefore be inefficient to expend limited agency resources on

DeepGreen’s application for a preliminary permit.

       In April 2026, the Maine State Legislature voted to approve a bill, L.D. 307, that would

have banned state and municipal permitting of data centers with a load of 20 MW or more until

November 1, 2027. 9 Governor Janet Mills vetoed L.D. 307, but only because the bill “fail[ed] to

allow for a specific project in the Town of Jay that enjoys strong local support from its host

community and region.” 10 The governor stated that, had the bill exempted that project from the

temporary moratorium, she would have signed it. 11 Formed by executive order shortly thereafter,

the Maine Data Center Advisory Council is currently preparing a report that will include

recommendations, including proposed legislation, that it will submit to the newly elected

governor and legislature by January 29, 2027. 12 Meanwhile, public opposition to data centers

continues to rise. A recent UMass Lowell poll found that, as of late August to mid-September

2026, 76% of Mainers oppose A.I. data center construction in their communities, with 58%

strongly opposing it (up from 51% in June). 13 Considering how close L.D. 307 came to passage




8
  16 U.S.C. § 802(a)(2).
9
  LD 307 (2025), “An Act to Establish the Maine Data Center Coordination Council and Place a
Temporary Limitation on Certain Data Centers.”
10
   Veto of Maine LD 307 (2025) (letter from Gov. Janet T. Mills to 132nd Legislature, Apr. 24, 2026),
https://www.maine.gov/governor/mills/official_documents/veto_messages/2026-04-ld-307-act-establish-
maine-data-center-coordination.
11
   Id.
12
   Maine Data Center Advisory Council, MAINE.GOV, https://www.maine.gov/energy/datacentercouncil
(last visited Oct. 14, 2026).
13
   Survey of Maine Likely Voters Aug. 28 to Sept. 14, 2026, UMASS LOWELL CTR. FOR PUB. OPINION,
https://www.uml.edu/docs/2026-Sept-Maine-Highlights_tcm18-422749.pdf (last visited Oct. 14, 2026).
                                                  3
 in early 2026 and escalating public opposition to data centers since then, future legislation to

significantly restrict, if not ban, data center construction seems likely. DeepGreen is thus unlikely

to satisfy Section 9’s requirement of compliance with applicable state law.

        In addition, in comments on this docket, the City of Eastport opposed DeepGreen’s

application and highlighted the current and future drain on municipal resources from responding

to the application, the lack of evidence that granting a preliminary permit would serve the public

interest, and unresolved questions about the environmental effects and financial and

technological viability. 14 In September 2026, in response to DeepGreen’s application, the

Eastport City Council also unanimously enacted ordinance provisions to ban large-scale data

centers in Eastport. 15 The City of Eastport’s comments emphasized that the City Council also

“expects to undertake additional work to strengthen and clarify the City’s protections.” 16 The

City of Eastport has motioned to intervene in this docket. 17 Even without any restrictions at the

state level (a scenario that, as described above, seems unlikely), the Underwater Data Center

lacks local support.

        Granting a preliminary permit for a project that will likely fail to satisfy Section 9’s

requirement to comply with state law to obtain a license—and that the relevant local community

opposes—would be irrational and wasteful.




14
   Fed. Energy Regul. Comm’n Docket P-15424-000, Comments of the Eastport City Council in
Opposition to the Application for Preliminary Permit (Sept. 22, 2026).
15
   Id. at 3.
16
   Id.; In restricting data center construction, the City of Eastport joins, by one tracker’s count, at least 14
other municipalities across the state that have banned data center construction and eight others that have
proposed similar limitations. Maine Data Center Moratorium Tracker, SAVRN (last updated Oct. 2026),
https://savrn.com/data-center-moratorium-tracker/maine (excluding Lewiston from the count of
municipalities with in-force bans, because Lewiston appears to have only rejected a specific proposed
data center, rather than issuing a broader ban).
17
   Fed. Energy Regul. Comm’n Docket P-15424-000, City of Eastport, Maine Motion to Intervene (Sept.
29, 2026).
                                                       4
      II.      The Proposed Project Should Not Proceed Because of the Negative Impacts on
              the Marine Environment, Including North Atlantic Right Whales and
              Commercially Important Fish Species.

           The Bay of Fundy is a highly productive marine ecosystem characterized by rich

biodiversity and a diverse array of habitats. 18 The area is known for having the world’s highest

recorded tides that cause cold, nutrient-rich water to move to the surface attracting the many

species that inhabit the area including large amounts of plankton and forage fish that serve as

vital components of the food web. 19 The rocky shore in the region allows for seaweed and other

fauna to flourish, creating important habitats. 20 Issuance of permits for any anthropogenic

activities in the Bay of Fundy should consider the adverse impacts to this important marine

ecosystem and the especially vulnerable species that us it. Notably, the endangered North

Atlantic right whale and several commercially and biologically important fish species could be

negatively impacted if the preliminary permit for DeepGreen’s Underwater Data Center is

granted.

              a.   The Proposed Project Would Adversely Impact North Atlantic Right Whales.

           The location of the proposed Underwater Data Center is cause for concern even at the

preliminary permit stage, because it would cause harm to the surrounding natural environment

and its inhabitants, including the North Atlantic right whale—a species listed an “endangered”

and protected under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). FERC would therefore be required to

initiate consultation with the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) on impacts to right

whales and, if necessary, obtain an incidental take permit under the ESA, including ensuring that


18
   Graham R. Dabord, The Bay of Fundy and its Future, Acadia University, 14-15, (Sep. 2018),
https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Peter-Wells-6/publication/327867867_PROCEEDINGS-2018-
Workshop_forWeb-1/links/5baa4e2992851ca9ed2512aa/PROCEEDINGS-2018-Workshop-forWeb-
1.pdf#page=13.
19
   Id.
20
   Id.
                                                  5
 DeepGreen has obtained an incidental take permit under the Marine Mammal Protection Act

(MMPA).

       ESA Section 7 requires NOAA to consult with the National Marine Fisheries Service

(NMFS) before authorizing an action that may affect ESA-listed species or their critical habitat.

See 16 U.S.C. § 1536(a)(2), (c). Actions that are likely to adversely affect a listed species require

formal consultation, which culminates in issuing a biological opinion determining—based on

“the best scientific and commercial data available”—whether the proposed action will jeopardize

a listed species or destroy or adversely modify designated critical habitat. 16 U.S.C. §

1536(a)(2), (b)(3)(A). Any actions that are likely to “take” an ESA-protected species require

FERC to obtain an incidental take permit under the ESA. Before FERC may obtain a take permit

under the ESA, DeepGreen must first obtain any required incidental take permit under the

MMPA. 16 U.S.C. § 1371(a); Ctr. for Biological Diversity v. Ross, 613 F. Supp. 3d 336, 341

(D.D.C. 2020).

       There are fewer than 400 North Atlantic right whales (and only 70 breeding females) left

and the death of even a single whale pushes the species closer to extinction. 21 Their two main

threats are vessel strikes and entanglement and new ocean activities that further increase

localized vessel traffic or adds infrastructure to the water column threaten both their survival and

recovery. 22 Right whales are also impacted by changes in water temperature that adversely affect

their prey—small crustaceans called copepods. 23 In the context of climate change, scientists have



21
   NMFS, North Atlantic Right Whale 5-Year Review: Summary ad Evaluation, 29, (Nov. 2022)
https://media.fisheries.noaa.gov/2022-12/Sign2_NARW20225YearReview_508-GARFO.pdf.
22
   NMFS, North Atlantic Right Whale, https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/north-atlantic-right-whale
(last updated July 29, 2026).
23
   Nicholas R. Record, et al., Rapid Climate-Driven Circulation Changes Threaten Conservation of
Endangered North Atlantic Right Whales¸ 32 Oceanography Society, 162-169 (June 2019)
https://www.jstor.org/stable/26651192?seq=3.
                                                   6
 documented fewer copepods in warmer waters; for right whales, an absence of adequate prey can

result in foraging displacement and energetic costs that could be difficult to overcome. 24 Data

centers generate an enormous amount of heat and here, where the Underwater Data Center plans

to discharge large volumes of thermal pollution back into the ocean, the potential downstream

consequences to copepods as well as the entirety of the marine ecosystem are cause for

significant concern. The Underwater Data Center plans request a 400-acre thermal dilution zone,

but the assumptions that went into to determining that area size and the potential impacts are

unknown at this time.

           Extensive data over the last 25 years demonstrates that North Atlantic right whales

regularly use the Bay of Fundy and surrounding areas. Thus, any activities associated with this

proposal may have adverse impacts on the species. See Figure 1 below.




Figure 1: WhaleMap.org; North Atlantic right whale presence in the Bay of Fundy from Oct. 19,
2018 – Oct. 19, 2026. Orange circle indicates the approximate area of the proposed project.




24
     Id.
                                                   7
        In U.S. waters, most of the Gulf of Maine is designated as critical habitat for North

Atlantic right whales under the Endangered Species Act because of its importance as foraging

grounds. In Canadian waters, the Grand Manan Basin at the mouth of the Bay of Fundy is

designated as critical habitat for right whales under the Species At Risk Act and considered a

vital foraging area because dense patches of Calanus finmarchicus (their primary food source)

are concentrated there due to strong tidal currents. 25 While the boundaries of the Proposed

Project appear to fall just outside designated critical habitat for right whales, the project’s

proximity to such critical habitat would nevertheless impact right whales and their food

sources—both from thermal and noise pollution and increased vessel traffic within the project

area itself and, possibly, extending into nearby designated critical habitat as well.

       Even to assess the feasibility of the project, DeepGreen will need to engage in activities

that disturb the project site and surrounding areas. Bathymetric and geophysical surveying will

increase vessel traffic and the risk of vessel strikes. Surveying will also increase ocean noise

potentially interfering with right whale communication and “reduc[ing] their ability to detect and

avoid predators and human hazards, navigate, identify physical surroundings, find food, and find

mates.” 26 As such, even before construction or operation of the proposed Underwater Data

Center (which will also increase vessel traffic and ocean noise), there are likely to be direct

adverse impacts on endangered North Atlantic right whales.

       FERC should not authorize this project or issue a preliminary permit. Should FERC

nevertheless proceed with permitting, it must first consult with NMFS under ESA Section 7



25
   Kimberley Davies, et al., Oceanographic Connectivity Between Right Whale Critical Habitats in
Canada and its Influence on Whale Abundance Indices During 1987-2009, J. Marine Systems (Oct.
2015), https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0924796315001050.
26
   NMFS, North Atlantic Right Whale, https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/species/north-atlantic-right-whale
(last updated July 29, 2026).
                                                   8
 regarding impacts on right whales and obtain any necessary incidental take permit under the

ESA, including ensuring that DeepGreen has obtained any necessary incidental take permit

under the MMPA.

            b. The Proposed Project Would Adversely Impact Important Fish Species and their
               Habitat.

        The waters of the Western Passage in the Bay of Fundy, surrounding the Town of

Eastport, are explicitly designated as essential fish habitat (EFH) for numerous commercially

important species, including Atlantic cod, Atlantic herring, Atlantic sea scallops, pollock, and

winter flounder. 27 This area is also EFH for the endangered Gulf of Maine Distinct Population

Segment of Atlantic Salmon and serves as an important emigration and immigration habitat for

individuals migrating between the Atlantic Ocean and their spawning habitat upstream. 28

        The Western Passage, where the DeepGreen quests 400 acres for the proposed project,

features complex rocky substrates, critical macroalgae cover, and intense tidal currents, and

serves as a vital nursery, feeding, and spawning ground for these species, and increased vessel

traffic, noise pollution, and other activities that physically alter the sea floor (such as silt scour

engineering) could all negatively impact the vital fish habitat necessary to sustain productive

fisheries. 29 Many of these species are overfished and/or subject to overfishing and require

conservation and management measures to rebuild according to the NOAA Fisheries. Activities



27
   NMFS, Essential Fish Habitat Mapper, https://www.habitat.noaa.gov/apps/efhmapper/?page=NEMA-
Map (Turn on layer: Essential Fish Habitat; Mid-Atlantic & New England EFH Species).
28
   NMFS, Essential Fish Habitat Mapper, https://www.habitat.noaa.gov/apps/efhmapper/?page=NEMA-
Map (Turn on layer: Essential Fish Habitat; Atlantic salmon EFH); New England Fishery Management
Council, NEFMC EFH Designations Developed as Part of Omnibus Essential Fish Habitat Amendment
2, (July 2017), https://d23h0vhsm26o6d.cloudfront.net/NEFMC_EFH_Designations.pdf.
29
   Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, Anthropogenic Noise Impacts on Atlantic Fish and
Fisheries: Implications for Managers and Long-Term Productivity, (Aug. 2024) https://asmfc.org/wp-
content/uploads/2024/12/HMS17_AnthropogenicNoiseImpacts.pdf; Marc Ayoub, Michael Flannagan &
Gesche Kindermann, Environmental and social impacts of tidal energy developments: A review, Energy
Reports (Dec. 2026) https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352484726003914.
                                                    9
 that interfere with EFH could have adverse impacts on the species that NOAA is working to

rebuild and the fisheries that rely on sustainable fish stocks for their livelihoods.

        Moreover, some of the fish in the area are acoustically sensitive. For example, Atlantic

cod use sound to communicate during “territorial behavior, courtship, and spawning” as well as

to “monitor the soundscape, detect prey, and avoid predators.” 30 Therefore, like North Atlantic

right whales, Atlantic cod and other fish species that rely on hearing for biological functions, will

be negatively impacted by the noise associated with increased vessel traffic and surveying

activities.

                                                 ***

        For the reasons explained above, FERC should deny DeepGreen’s preliminary permit and

protect the marine ecosystem and the people and industries that rely on it.



DATED: October 19, 2026


                                                       Respectfully submitted,

                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


In the Matter of the Application of:               )
                                                   )
DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC                  )               Docket No. P-15424-000


                           CONSERVATION LAW FOUNDATION
                               MOTION TO INTERVENE
        Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Rules and Regulations of the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission (the “Commission” or “FERC”), Conservation Law Foundation (“CLF”) hereby

moves to intervene in the above-captioned proceeding regarding the preliminary permit

application (“Permit Application”) filed by DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC

(“DeepGreen”) for the DeepGreen Western Passage Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub

Project (FERC Project No. 15424-000) ("Underwater Data Center"). 18 C.F.R. § 385.214. By this

motion, CLF seeks to pursue its interests, those of its members, and the public interest at large, by

protecting sensitive ecosystems that support important marine wildlife, local jobs, and sustainable

fisheries, as FERC evaluates this application.

                                  CONTACT INFORMATION

        All filings, orders, and correspondence regarding these proceedings and this intervention

should be addressed to:


               Erin Shortell
               Conservation Law Foundation
               53 Exchange St, Suite 200
               Portland, ME 4101
               (207) 228-2730
               eshortell@clf.org

   I.      DESCRIPTION OF INTERVENOR

        Founded in 1966, CLF is a non-profit advocacy organization with over 8,300 members

                                                  1
 across New England, including over 500 in Maine. CLF works to solve the environmental

problems threatening the people, natural resources, and communities of New England. CLF’s

advocates use law, economics, and science to design and implement strategies that conserve

natural resources, protect public health, and promote vital communities in our region. CLF has

members in many of the communities that border the Gulf of Maine and Bay of Fundy, including

in Eastport, the site of the proposed Underwater Data Center.

       For decades, CLF has worked to restore habitat along New England’s coasts and in the

wider ocean environment, for important species such as the endangered North Atlantic right

whale, Fin whale, Humpback whale, and Atlantic cod. By working to protect important ocean

habitats, such as the Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument, along with

ongoing efforts to protect Cashes Ledge, CLF strives to support thriving ocean ecosystems and

sustainable fisheries for a vibrant future.

       CLF and its members may be adversely affected by the outcome of this proceeding.

Members of CLF use the Gulf of Maine and Bay of Fundy for recreational, commercial,

educational, and aesthetic pursuits. CLF members are part of the commercial lobster fishery in

Eastport, while others fish recreationally, and otherwise enjoy the ocean in the vicinity of Eastport

and the Western Passage. In addition to fishermen, CLF members include Maine Guides that earn

income showing visitors the natural environment along Maine’s coast, including in sea kayaks.

These industries are important to the livelihood of CLF’s members and the area’s economy. Even

a preliminary study—which would involve the use of sonar and other disruptive marine survey

methods—could affect sensitive habitat. Construction and operation of the Underwater Data

Center would pose even greater risks, including the potential for habitat destruction and vessel

collisions. These effects would likely impair CLF members’ ability to earn a living, enjoy their

local environment, and would negatively impact the community as a whole. Thus, CLF has a

                                                  2
 strong, direct interest in preventing these harms.

    II.       THE PROPOSED PROJECT

           According to FERC’s own summary of DeepGreen’s application following its

amendments on June 8 and July 30, 2026,

           “The proposed project would consist of the following new features: (1) a 3.5-meter-
           high and 24-meter-wide subsea modular universal docking cradle; (2) thirty-four 12-
           meter-long and 4.2-meter-diameter subsea compute pods; (3) a 1.8-meter-diameter
           spherical and elevated tidal sensing power platform; (4) up to 16 marine hydrokinetic
           turbine-generator units, each rated at 300-kilowatt (kW); and (5) a 1.5-mile-long
           hybrid power-and-fiber subsea cable operating at 13.8 kilovolts (kV). The proposed
           project would be configured as a behind-the-meter captive generation loop without
           a grid connection.” 1

According to the Center for Biological Diversity, the project could expand to occupy as many as

400 acres, with up to thirty-four turbines and a combined output of ten to fifteen megawatts of

electricity. 2 Before any of that construction takes place, the preliminary permit phase would

involve project exploration using “high-resolution bathymetric and geophysical surveys, mapping,

year-round environmental monitoring,” 3 and other studies, all of which would be highly disruptive

to the environment and local community.

    III.      GROUNDS FOR INTERVENTION

           Pursuant to FERC Rule 214, prospective intervenors must state their position, along with

that position’s basis in law and in fact. 4 Rule 214 further requires that the movant state its interest

in sufficient factual detail to demonstrate that the movant represents “an interest which may be

directly affected by the outcome of the proceeding” or that “[its] participation is in the public



1
  FERC, Notice of Preliminary Permit Application Accepted for Filing and Soliciting Comments, Motions to
Intervene, and Competing Applications, Doc. No. P-15424-000, at 1 (Aug. 19, 2026).
2
  Ctr. For Biological Diversity, Motion to Intervene, Doc. No. P-15424-000, at 3 (Sept. 24, 2026) (citing FERC,
DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC; Notice of Preliminary Permit Application Accepted for Filing and Soliciting
Comments, Motions to Intervene, and Competing Applications, Doc. No. P-15424-000 (Aug. 25, 2026).
3
  Id.
4
  18 C.F.R. § 385.214(b)(1).

                                                       3
 interest.” 5 The proposed Underwater Data Center would directly interfere with the interests of

CLF and its members. The Western Passage, in which the Underwater Data Center would be

located, is a vital marine environment that supports the endangered North Atlantic right whale and

many other species. CLF members have strong interests in the health of marine ecosystems. With

less than 400 right whales left, CLF and its members have spent decades working hard to protect

the species from vessel strikes and entanglement.

        Moreover, disturbances caused by studies conducted at the preliminary-permit stage

(which would include the use of sonar and other disruptive survey equipment and would be likely

to increase vessel traffic in the area), as well as any later construction or operation of the

Underwater Data Center, is likely to adversely affect that marine habitat, heighten the risk of

vessel collisions, and otherwise disrupt the marine economy and ecosystem. All those outcomes

will harm CLF and its members’ interests.

        Further, CLF members in Eastport have a deep organizational interest in the Commission’s

consideration of the preliminary permit, which, if granted, would “secure priority of application

for a license” going forward. 6 Such preferential treatment is especially unwarranted in light of the

City of Eastport’s own opposition to the project, highlighted by its unanimous enactment, in

September 2026, of an ordinance banning large-scale data center development in the city. 7 In

short, given the unproven nature of the technology the project will rely on, local opposition, and

likely environmental impacts, further consideration of the project wastes time and limited agency

resources. Such consideration would cast a pall over any other, more realistic and beneficial



5
  Id. Finally, this motion is submitted before the October 19, 2026 deadline established by FERC and is therefore
timely. See FERC, Notice of Preliminary Permit Application Accepted for Filing and Soliciting Comments, Motions to
Intervene, and Competing Applications, Doc. No. P-15424-000 (Aug. 25, 2026).
6
  18 CFR § 4.80; see also 16 U.S.C. § 798(a).
7
  Fed. Energy Regul. Comm’n Docket P-15424-000, Comments of the Eastport City Council in Opposition to the
Application for Preliminary Permit 3 (Sept. 22, 2026).

                                                        4
 development in the Eastport area.

          In sum, CLF and its members have a direct and substantial interest in these proceedings.

Intervention would allow CLF to mitigate harm to critical wildlife habitat, the local economy, and

its own members’ livelihoods.

    IV.      STATEMENT OF POSITION

          CLF seeks to intervene to ensure that important public resources are protected. As stated,

these resources include habitat for the endangered North Atlantic right whale and other species,

along with the recreational and commercial benefits associated with a marine environment

untainted by large-scale underwater infrastructure projects. Should this project advance past the

preliminary permitting stage, CLF seeks to ensure that any future development complies with all

applicable federal and state environmental laws. CLF intends to protect the public interest, and the

interests of its members, by opposing the preliminary permit and the harm it would cause to those

interests.

    V.       CONCLUSION

          The above information demonstrates CLF’s and its members’ direct and substantial interest

in the outcome of the preliminary permit application that has been filed with the Commission for

the DeepGreen Western Passage Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub, FERC Project No.

15424-000. For the foregoing reasons, Conservation Law Foundation should be permitted to

intervene with full rights in this proceeding.


DATED: October 19, 2026




                                                   5
     Respectfully submitted,



    __________________________
    Sean Mahoney, Esq.
    Vice President and Senior Counsel for Maine

       On February 11, 2026, DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC (DeepGreen) filed an

modified and supplemented its application on June 8, 2026 and July 30, 2026. 1 In its application,

DeepGreen proposed to study the feasibility of the DeepGreen Western Passage Subsea-Compute

& Infrastructure Hub Project No. 15424-000 (Underwater Data Center). 2 The proposed

Underwater Data Center would be located in the Bay of Fundy, near the City of Eastport,

Maine. 3 On August 19, 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) accepted the

application for filing and requested public comment. 4

preliminary permit application. The comments raise two main arguments. First, given the

likelihood of a statewide ban or other limitations on data center construction in Maine as well as

unreasonable and inefficient to grant DeepGreen’s application. Second, the proposed project

    I.      Given the Likelihood of Statewide Restrictions on Data Center Construction and
            Local Opposition to the Underwater Data Center, Granting DeepGreen’s
            Preliminary Permit Application Would Be Unreasonable and Inefficient.

         Water power developers regulated by the Federal Power Act sometimes lack the Section 9

information needed to apply for a project license. To address this problem, Section 4(f)

authorizes FERC to issue a preliminary permit to a project developer. 5 The preliminary permit

“secure[s] priority of application for a license for a water power project . . . while the permittee

obtains the data and performs the acts required to determine the feasibility of the project and to

support an application for a license.” 6 If a project developer is unlikely to meet Section 9’s

requirements for a license, however, granting a preliminary permit under Section 4(f) is illogical

and specious.

         Such is the case here. DeepGreen seeks a preliminary permit under Section 4(f) to study

the proposed Underwater Data Center’s feasibility. 7 But under Section 9, to receive a license

from FERC to actually build the Underwater Data Center, DeepGreen would also need to submit

“[s]atisfactory evidence” that it has complied with Maine law “with respect to bed and banks and

to the appropriation, diversion, and use of water for power purposes and with respect to the right

to engage in the business of developing, transmitting, and distributing power, and in any other

      II.      The Proposed Project Should Not Proceed Because of the Negative Impacts on
              the Marine Environment, Including North Atlantic Right Whales and
              Commercially Important Fish Species.

           The Bay of Fundy is a highly productive marine ecosystem characterized by rich

biodiversity and a diverse array of habitats. 18 The area is known for having the world’s highest

recorded tides that cause cold, nutrient-rich water to move to the surface attracting the many

species that inhabit the area including large amounts of plankton and forage fish that serve as

vital components of the food web. 19 The rocky shore in the region allows for seaweed and other

fauna to flourish, creating important habitats. 20 Issuance of permits for any anthropogenic

activities in the Bay of Fundy should consider the adverse impacts to this important marine

ecosystem and the especially vulnerable species that us it. Notably, the endangered North

Atlantic right whale and several commercially and biologically important fish species could be

negatively impacted if the preliminary permit for DeepGreen’s Underwater Data Center is

granted.

              a.   The Proposed Project Would Adversely Impact North Atlantic Right Whales.

           The location of the proposed Underwater Data Center is cause for concern even at the

preliminary permit stage, because it would cause harm to the surrounding natural environment

and its inhabitants, including the North Atlantic right whale—a species listed an “endangered”

and protected under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). FERC would therefore be required to

initiate consultation with the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) on impacts to right

whales and, if necessary, obtain an incidental take permit under the ESA, including ensuring that

       ESA Section 7 requires NOAA to consult with the National Marine Fisheries Service

(NMFS) before authorizing an action that may affect ESA-listed species or their critical habitat.

See 16 U.S.C. § 1536(a)(2), (c). Actions that are likely to adversely affect a listed species require

formal consultation, which culminates in issuing a biological opinion determining—based on

“the best scientific and commercial data available”—whether the proposed action will jeopardize

a listed species or destroy or adversely modify designated critical habitat. 16 U.S.C. §

1536(a)(2), (b)(3)(A). Any actions that are likely to “take” an ESA-protected species require

FERC to obtain an incidental take permit under the ESA. Before FERC may obtain a take permit

under the ESA, DeepGreen must first obtain any required incidental take permit under the

MMPA. 16 U.S.C. § 1371(a); Ctr. for Biological Diversity v. Ross, 613 F. Supp. 3d 336, 341

(D.D.C. 2020).

       There are fewer than 400 North Atlantic right whales (and only 70 breeding females) left

and the death of even a single whale pushes the species closer to extinction. 21 Their two main

threats are vessel strikes and entanglement and new ocean activities that further increase

localized vessel traffic or adds infrastructure to the water column threaten both their survival and

recovery. 22 Right whales are also impacted by changes in water temperature that adversely affect

their prey—small crustaceans called copepods. 23 In the context of climate change, scientists have

        In U.S. waters, most of the Gulf of Maine is designated as critical habitat for North

Atlantic right whales under the Endangered Species Act because of its importance as foraging

grounds. In Canadian waters, the Grand Manan Basin at the mouth of the Bay of Fundy is

designated as critical habitat for right whales under the Species At Risk Act and considered a

vital foraging area because dense patches of Calanus finmarchicus (their primary food source)

are concentrated there due to strong tidal currents. 25 While the boundaries of the Proposed

Project appear to fall just outside designated critical habitat for right whales, the project’s

proximity to such critical habitat would nevertheless impact right whales and their food

sources—both from thermal and noise pollution and increased vessel traffic within the project

area itself and, possibly, extending into nearby designated critical habitat as well.

       Even to assess the feasibility of the project, DeepGreen will need to engage in activities

that disturb the project site and surrounding areas. Bathymetric and geophysical surveying will

increase vessel traffic and the risk of vessel strikes. Surveying will also increase ocean noise

potentially interfering with right whale communication and “reduc[ing] their ability to detect and

avoid predators and human hazards, navigate, identify physical surroundings, find food, and find

mates.” 26 As such, even before construction or operation of the proposed Underwater Data

Center (which will also increase vessel traffic and ocean noise), there are likely to be direct

adverse impacts on endangered North Atlantic right whales.

            b. The Proposed Project Would Adversely Impact Important Fish Species and their
               Habitat.

        The waters of the Western Passage in the Bay of Fundy, surrounding the Town of

Eastport, are explicitly designated as essential fish habitat (EFH) for numerous commercially

important species, including Atlantic cod, Atlantic herring, Atlantic sea scallops, pollock, and

winter flounder. 27 This area is also EFH for the endangered Gulf of Maine Distinct Population

Segment of Atlantic Salmon and serves as an important emigration and immigration habitat for

individuals migrating between the Atlantic Ocean and their spawning habitat upstream. 28

        The Western Passage, where the DeepGreen quests 400 acres for the proposed project,

features complex rocky substrates, critical macroalgae cover, and intense tidal currents, and

serves as a vital nursery, feeding, and spawning ground for these species, and increased vessel

traffic, noise pollution, and other activities that physically alter the sea floor (such as silt scour

engineering) could all negatively impact the vital fish habitat necessary to sustain productive

fisheries. 29 Many of these species are overfished and/or subject to overfishing and require

conservation and management measures to rebuild according to the NOAA Fisheries. Activities

        Moreover, some of the fish in the area are acoustically sensitive. For example, Atlantic

cod use sound to communicate during “territorial behavior, courtship, and spawning” as well as

to “monitor the soundscape, detect prey, and avoid predators.” 30 Therefore, like North Atlantic

right whales, Atlantic cod and other fish species that rely on hearing for biological functions, will

be negatively impacted by the noise associated with increased vessel traffic and surveying

activities.

        For the reasons explained above, FERC should deny DeepGreen’s preliminary permit and

protect the marine ecosystem and the people and industries that rely on it.
